To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Alzheimer disease is the most common cause of dementia worldwide; 2) the disease is preceded by an asymptomatic phase that can be measured by biomarkers; and 3) current therapeutic trials have failed to prevent the progression of the disease.

1) the apolipoprotein e &egr;4 gene allele is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer disease, 2) the disease is preceded by decades of cerebral amyloid and tau accumulation, 3) amyloid‐targeted immunotherapy has been unsuccessful to date, and 4) future trials in asymptomatic individuals at genetic risk for Alzheimer disease offer hope of earlier and more effective intervention.

the most prevalent form of dementia is a disease that has a long, pre‐clinical phase, during which the brain undergoes progressive pathological changes, that the pathological changes can now be detected antemortem, that these changes can be reversed by immunotherapeutic approaches in animal models and, to a lesser extent, in humans, that the pathological process is driven by amyloid and tau, and that the disease is caused by a complex interaction of multiple genetic and environmental risk factors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pathophysiological changes in the brain that occur with aging, and the mechanisms that lead to the development of Alzheimer’s disease.
the molecular mechanisms of Alzheimer disease (AD), and with the development of therapeutic strategies that can prevent or delay its onset and progression.
the development of a new approach to the study of the development of disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
AD has been extensively researched, and we know much about it, but we still have much to learn.
the field of AD research has made enormous progress in the past decade but that the translation of this progress into clinical benefit has yet to be achieved.
we know more about the biology of AD than ever before, and yet we are still no closer to a cure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AD is a disease of the brain and that it is a disease of genes, but also that it is a complex disease of the brain, a disease of the genes, and a disease of the body.
we have come a very long way, but there is a long way to go.
the amyloid hypothesis is still a good hypothesis, but the clinical trials are still not good enough.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the field is now poised to move from the study of symptomatic AD to that of its prodromal and preclinical stages, which offer a unique opportunity to test the amyloid cascade hypothesis and to develop disease‐modifying treatments for AD.
the AD field is in a state of flux, and we should be prepared for surprises.
AD is a complex, slowly progressing, multifaceted disorder that is not a single disease but a collection of diseases with different underlying causes and different rates and patterns of progression.
